title: Prepare the heart (Berakhot 30b)
hookLine: the early pious waited before praying to direct their hearts
tomorrow: a priest thinks a praying woman is drunk. why?

cards: Athletes have pre-game routines: the same playlist, the same laces, a quiet minute in the tunnel. The Mishnah describes something like that before prayer. The early pious ones, it says, would wait an hour and then pray.
Waiting for what? So they could direct their hearts to their Father in heaven. But how should that heart arrive, heavy or glad?
Inside the tradition, there are two answers.

teach.b: The Mishnah's own phrase is koved rosh, a heavy head: seriousness, weight. Don't stand to pray lightly. Here's its best case.
You're about to stand before God, and someone who walks in mid-joke, still scrolling, hasn't arrived yet. The early pious took that so seriously they gave it an hour.

teach.h: THE OTHER: THE JOY OF A MITZVAH.
teach.b: Now the other voice, a few lines on in the Talmud. One shouldn't stand to pray out of sadness, or laziness, or laughter, or idle chatter, but out of the joy of a mitzvah. Here's its best case.
If prayer always comes with a heavy head, it turns into dread, and dread is a strange way to come to a Father in heaven. So which is it? The Talmud doesn't choose.

teach.h: SERVE WITH FEAR, REJOICE WITH TREMBLING.
teach.b: It quotes a psalm that holds both in one line: "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling." Gravity and gladness, in the same breath. Both voices agree on the real point.
The heart isn't being prepared for a mood.
It's being pointed, turned toward someone. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the early pious gave the moment before prayer as much care as the prayer itself.

how: Before the Amidah, it is customary to take a few small steps forward and stand with feet together; some pause first, or say a verse, to direct the heart.

o: write your request out before you say it aloud
wash your hands and face before saying a blessing
pause first, so the heart arrives before the words

games.q: two ways to arrive — tap the pairs.

s: Jewish prayer is meant to be gloomy and heavy
the Talmud: pray out of the joy of a mitzvah; the psalm: rejoice with trembling.
the early pious waited before praying to direct their hearts
the Mishnah says they waited an hour, toward their Father in heaven.
the Talmud settles it: seriousness wins over joy
it keeps both, and quotes 'serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.'

games.q: your friend says prayer should always feel solemn, never cheerful. what's the best case for the other side, from inside the tradition?
o: the Talmud: pray out of the joy of a mitzvah, not sadness or laziness.
the Mishnah: the early pious laughed together before they prayed.
the psalm: serve the LORD with gladness only, and never with fear.
games.why: Berakhot 31a: not from sadness, laziness, laughter or idle talk, but from the joy of a mitzvah. the Talmud keeps it beside the Mishnah's heavy head.

practice: Stand if you can, feet together and hands loose, the way people stand for the Amidah. Before saying anything, wait a full minute there, letting your mind arrive where your body already is.
Then notice which heart showed up today: heavy, glad, or both.

wordCard.voice: Prepare the heart. The early pious waited before praying to direct their hearts to their Father in heaven, with seriousness and with joy.

orig.note: Hebrew: heaviness of head, seriousness. the Mishnah's word for how to stand to pray.

carryVoice: Your line: prepare the heart. Heavy, glad, or both, it arrives before the words. Twenty-one of fifty.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 5:1, Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 30b (koved rosh; the early pious waited an hour to direct their hearts)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 31a (not from sadness, laziness, laughter or idle talk, but from the joy of a mitzvah)

sources.q: Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
